Practice can help you find words. These Berkeley resources offer information, education, and support beyond an example conversation.

Berkeley campus resources

UHS Sexual Health Care

Information about partner communication, STI testing, contraception, and access to sexual-health care.

When you have a sexual-health question or want to explore care options.

Start here: Open the UHS guide and choose Get Tested to compare testing and care options. A clinician can help with individual questions.

Sexual Health Education Program (SHEP)

Peer sexual-health education, answers to questions, and safer-sex resources.

When you would like to talk with a trained peer educator.

Start here: Use MyUCBerkeleyHealth to schedule a Sexpert Education Clinic appointment, or check the SHEP page for current walk-in hours.

PATH to Care: student prevention

Education on consent, boundaries, and healthy relationships.

When you want to learn more about relationship communication and consent.

Start here: Open the student prevention page to explore Consent & Boundaries workshops and the workshop request form for your group.

Check each service's page for current availability and appointment details.

From class to conversation

What we apply from PBHLTH 182.

Learning objective K asks us to examine communication in romantic and sexual relationships, including conflict and culture. These stories turn that learning into choices you can try and revisit.

Speak from your own experience

DIS 103 Meeting #6 introduced “I” statements and questions that invite a partner's perspective. In Sexual preferences, compare a statement about your own comfort with wording that can sound like criticism.

Check understanding and leave room to pause

Meeting #6 also emphasized paraphrasing, clear boundaries, and future check-ins. In Protection, clarify what an agreement includes. In Consent & boundaries, practice changing your mind without promising a later activity.

Connect a health conversation to support

Meeting #8 connected STI prevention with partner communication and testing resources. In Sexual health, ask about testing without treating the question as an accusation, then find a campus service for individual questions.

Course sources: PBHLTH 182, Fall 2026, syllabus, learning objective K; DIS 103 (Melody), Meeting #6 and Meeting #8. Course files require bCourses access. The guides and practice on this website are open to everyone.

Our evidence and approach

Research informing the practice.

Berkeley UHS identifies sexual history, STI testing, protection, boundaries, and preferences as important topics for partner communication, and recognizes that these discussions can be challenging.

A survey of 1,349 college students across six US universities found that confidence, communication expectations, and perceived partner attitudes were associated with safer-sex communication. This observational study does not establish cause and effect or estimate how common a concern is among Berkeley students.

DiIorio, C., Dudley, W. N., Lehr, S., & Soet, J. E. (2000). Correlates of safer sex communication among college students. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 32(3), 658–665. Research abstract.

Research with young adults also highlights a need for practical scripts, conversation examples, and accessible education about sexual health and relationships. This informs our use of guided stories; it is not an evaluation of this website.

Gilbert, S., Rogers, J., Carmody, M., & McGovern, L. (2026; first published online 2025). Uncovering What Matters to Young Adults: Communicating About Sexual Health & Relationships. American Journal of Sexuality Education, 21(3), 279–301.

These research samples are not Berkeley-specific. Berkeley UHS, SHEP, and PATH to Care are campus information and support resources, distinct from the research cited above.

How we use that context

Our original contribution is a self-paced set of branching conversations, with adjustable coaching and opportunities to try another response. These four stories complement existing campus information and peer education by giving Berkeley students a place to rehearse wording, respond to misunderstandings, and navigate different needs. You can adapt the language to your own voice while respecting each person's boundaries and choices.

The intended benefit is clearer language and a useful next step. The project's effect on confidence or sexual-health behavior has not been established. A small usability test can help us improve wording and navigation; it cannot by itself demonstrate a health outcome.

The opening check-in suggests a level of guidance for practice. It is a personal reflection, not a validated assessment of communication skill. Before-and-after feelings are shown only to the person practicing and do not establish that the project caused a change.

About this project

Created for PBHLTH 182, discussion group 103-3, by Wenqi Zhang, Xuanyu Lin, Zijian Huang, and Yanghong Liu. The STI-testing example and four-topic structure build on our group proposal and pitch.

UHS, SHEP, and PATH to Care are existing campus resources. Linking to them does not imply a partnership or endorsement. Campus resource pages and the Gilbert et al. citation were rechecked November 25, 2026. Other research citations were checked November 19, 2026.
